name: Mia Thompson
presenting_complaint: Fever and irritability for 12 hours, now drowsy with a new spotty rash

conditions: Fully immunised for age, previously well
Born at term, no perinatal problems
medications: Paracetamol 120 mg given by parents 3 hours ago
medical_history.social: Lives with both parents, attends childcare. No recent travel. Estimated weight 12 kg.
medical_history.family: No significant family history. No known sick contacts, but a child at childcare recently unwell.

validation_criteria.presenting_scenario: A 2-year-old girl (estimated weight 12 kg) is brought to ED by her worried mother with 12 hours of high fever and irritability, now becoming drowsy and difficult to rouse. In the last hour the parents noticed a new spotty rash on her legs and trunk. She is mottled and poorly perfused with cool peripheries and a capillary refill of 4 seconds. Obs: temp 39.7, HR 182, RR 46, BP 78/42, SpO2 95% in air, GCS 13, BGL 2.4. The mother says 'she just isn't herself and this is not like her normal colds.'
validation_criteria.task: Document your assessment and initial management as the admitting RMO.

subjective: Fever history: onset, duration (12 hours), height, response to paracetamol; note antipyretic given so fever number may be masked
Take the parent's concern seriously: 'she isn't herself / not like her usual illnesses' is a red flag, not reassurance
Red-flag screen: drowsiness/reduced alertness, reduced feeding and urine output, new rash, no seizures, no neck stiffness reported, breathing effort
Source screen for occult focus: cough/coryza, ear pain, urine symptoms/offensive urine (urine is the most commonly missed source), abdominal pain, limp/joint
Risk factors for serious bacterial infection: age, immunisation status, unwell contacts at childcare, immunocompromise, recent antibiotics
Birth history, immunisation status, allergies and exact weight/dose of any medication already given
objective: Paediatric Assessment Triangle and full A-E: appearance (drowsy, GCS 13), work of breathing (RR 46), circulation (mottled, capillary refill 4 s, cool peripheries)
Examine the WHOLE undressed skin for a non-blanching petechial/purpuric rash and perform the glass/tumbler test — document blanching vs non-blanching
Bedside blood glucose immediately (documented 2.4 = hypoglycaemic in an unwell child) and repeat after treatment
Check for meningism/raised ICP signs: bulging fontanelle if open, neck stiffness, pupils, tone, focal neurology (guide safety of LP timing)
Full septic screen: FBC, UEC, CRP, blood cultures BEFORE or with first antibiotic dose, venous/capillary gas and lactate, coagulation profile, catheter/clean-catch urine microscopy and culture
Continuous cardiac/SpO2 monitoring, temperature, hourly obs and repeat capillary refill; weigh or estimate weight (12 kg) for all dosing
assessment: Serious bacterial infection with septic shock — meningococcal sepsis (meningococcaemia) until proven otherwise, given fever, drowsiness, non-blanching rash and poor perfusion
Consider bacterial meningitis as an overlapping diagnosis; LP deferred until child resuscitated and safe (do NOT delay antibiotics for LP)
Differentials: urinary tract infection/pyelonephritis, pneumonia, other bacteraemia; hypoglycaemia secondary to sepsis
This is a time-critical emergency — recognise decompensated shock (hypotension is a late, ominous sign in a toddler)
plan: FIRST: recognise septic child, high-flow oxygen, IV/IO access x2 within minutes and send cultures — treat the child, not the number
Empirical IV antibiotics WITHIN 1 HOUR (aim <15 min): ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg IV = 600 mg (max 2 g) — do NOT delay antibiotics for LP or CT
If IV access delayed, give benzylpenicillin 50 mg/kg (max 2 g) IM/IV or ceftriaxone IM immediately for suspected meningococcal disease
Correct hypoglycaemia now: 2 mL/kg of 10% dextrose IV = 24 mL, then recheck BGL
Fluid resuscitation: 10-20 mL/kg 0.9% sodium chloride IV bolus = 120-240 mL, reassess after each bolus for perfusion and signs of fluid overload; escalate to inotropes if shock persists
Paracetamol 15 mg/kg = 180 mg for comfort (not for the number); antipyretic must not be used to justify discharge
Escalate early: call paediatric registrar and PICU/retrieval immediately; as an adult-trained RMO involve paediatrics rather than manage alone

Admit; consider aciclovir if encephalitis suspected; defer LP until resuscitated, no coagulopathy and no raised-ICP/shock; notify public health and arrange meningococcal chemoprophylaxis for close contacts

critical_errors: Discharging or under-triaging this child because she briefly looks settled after paracetamol / because a single vital sign normalises — being reassured by a well-looking number in a worried parent's child
Delaying or withholding empirical IV/IM antibiotics (ceftriaxone or benzylpenicillin) to wait for LP, CT, or blood results in a child with suspected meningococcal sepsis
Failing to fully undress and examine the skin / missing the non-blanching purpuric rash and not treating meningococcaemia
Not checking the blood glucose in an unwell child, or failing to treat the documented hypoglycaemia (BGL 2.4) with IV dextrose
Performing a lumbar puncture before resuscitation in a shocked child with signs of raised ICP/coagulopathy
must_not_miss: Meningococcal sepsis / serious bacterial infection recognised and empirical antibiotics given within 1 hour
Non-blanching petechial/purpuric rash actively sought and identified (glass/tumbler test)
Hypoglycaemia identified and corrected (BGL checked in every unwell child)
Full septic screen including urine (most commonly missed source) and blood cultures taken at IV/IO insertion, with the first antibiotic dose — must NOT delay antibiotics
Early escalation to paediatric registrar/PICU/retrieval and contact chemoprophylaxis / public health notification
